'''Lynn Moorhead Riddiford''' (born 1936) is an American [[entomology|entomologist]] and developmental [[biologist]]. She was the first female faculty member in the Harvard Biology Department<ref name="jimorjack"/> where she served as an assistant and associate professor. She is an emeritus professor at the University of Washington. In 1997, she was the first awardee of the Recognition Award in Insect Physiology, Biochemistry, and Toxicology from the [[Entomological Society of America]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.entsoc.org/pbt/recognition-pbt-award-winners|title=Winners of the Recognition Award in Insect Physiology, Biochemistry, and Toxicology|website=Entomological Society of America|access-date=2 June 2018}}</ref> Riddiford studies the endocrinology of insects, specifically the [[Manduca sexta|tobacco hornworm]].

==Education==
Riddiford attended [[Radcliffe College]]. Her junior year, she joined [[Carroll Williams]]' lab at Harvard, where she began studying [[juvenile hormone]] in insects and other animals and plants. This work led to her first major publication in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' in 1959.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Williams|first1=Carroll|last2=Moorhead|first2=Lynn|last3=Pulis|first3=JF|title=Juvenile hormone in thymus, human placenta and other mammalian organs|journal=Nature|date=February 1959|volume=183|issue=4658|pages=405|bibcode=1959Natur.183..405W|doi=10.1038/183405a0|pmid=13632741|s2cid=4277439|doi-access=free}}</ref> She graduated in biochemical sciences in 1958. She received her Ph.D. in zoology at [[Cornell University]] in 1961, advised by Professors Marcus Singer and [[Harold Scheraga]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Riddiford |first1=Lynn |last2=Scheraga |first2=Harold |title=Structural studies of paramyosin. I. Hydrogen ion equilibria. |journal=Biochemistry |date=January 1962 |volume=1 |pages=95–107 |doi=10.1021/bi00907a015 |pmid=14492100}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Riddiford |first1=Lynn |last2=Scheraga |first2=Harold |title=Structural studies of paramyosin. II. Conformational changes. |journal=Biochemistry |date=January 1962 |volume=1 |pages=108–114 |doi=10.1021/bi00907a016 |pmid=14492101}}</ref>

==Career==
[[File:University of Washington Friday Harbor Laboratories 02 (20614327866).jpg|right|thumb|University of Washington Friday Harbor Marine Biology Laboratories]]
Riddiford returned to Harvard as a postdoctoral fellow in John Edsall's laboratory for two years.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Edsall |first1=John |title=Some Personal History and Reflections from the Life of a Biochemist |journal=Annual Review of Biochemistry |date=July 1971 |volume=40 |issue=1 |pages=1–29 |doi=10.1146/annurev.bi.40.070171.000245 |pmid=4941235|doi-access=free }}</ref> She then taught zoology at [[Wellesley College]] for two years.<ref>{{cite book |title=Bulletin of Wellesley College Catalogue Number 1963-1964 |date=30 October 1963 |publisher=Wellesley College |page=16 |url=https://repository.wellesley.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1061&context=catalogs |access-date=5 October 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Bulletin of Wellesley College Catalogue Number 1964-1965 |date=30 October 1964 |publisher=Wellesley College |page=16 |url=https://repository.wellesley.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1062&context=catalogs |access-date=5 October 2018}}</ref> In 1965, she returned to Harvard as a research associate in Williams's laboratory, then became an assistant professor in 1966 and associate professor in 1971 in the Harvard Biology Department. Her lab focused on the endocrinology of the [[tobacco hornworm]], ''Manduca sexta'', and led to key findings about the interplay of juvenile hormone and molting hormone.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Riddiford|first1=Lynn|last2=Truman|first2=James|year=1972|title=Delayed effects of juvenile hormone on insect metamorphosis are mediated by the corpus allatum|journal=Nature|volume=237|issue=5356|pages=458|doi=10.1038/237458a0|pmid=4557475|bibcode=1972Natur.237..458R|s2cid=4205651|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 1973, Riddiford moved to the Department of Zoology [[University of Washington]]. In 2007, she retired from the university and became a senior fellow at the Janelia Farm Research Campus of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. She retired from Janelia in 2016.<ref>{{cite web |title=Riddiford Lab |url=https://www.janelia.org/our-research/overview/former-labs#riddiford |website=Janelia Research Campus |access-date=5 October 2018}}</ref>

In 1979, Riddiford was awarded a [[John Simon Guggenheim Fellowship|John Simon Guggenheim fellowship]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/lynn-m-riddiford/|title=Lynn M. Riddiford|website=John Simon Guggenheim Foundation|access-date=2 June 2018}}</ref> In 1993 she was elected a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. In 2010, Riddiford became an elected member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gupta|first=Sujata|date=30 July 2013|title=QnAs with Lynn M. Riddiford|pmc=3732987|journal=Proc Natl Acad Sci USA|volume=110 |issue=31|pages=12501–12502|via=PMC|pmid=23878246|doi=10.1073/pnas.1311709110|bibcode=2013PNAS..11012501G|doi-access=free}}</ref>  In 2011, she was awarded the [[Howard Vollum Award]] for Distinguished Accomplishment in Science and Technology from [[Reed College]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.reed.edu/convocation/archive/2011/riddiford.html|title=Dr. Lynn Riddiford Vollum Award for Distinguished Accomplishment in Science and Technology 2011 recipient|website=Reed College|access-date=2 June 2018}}</ref> In June 2018, Riddiford was elected to the Washington Academy of Science for significant contributions to the field of developmental biology.<ref>{{cite news |title=Press Release |url=http://www.washacad.org/new-members-press-release/ |access-date=5 October 2018 |publisher=Washington State Academy of Science |date=13 July 2018}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Riddiford married [[James W. Truman|James Truman]], her former graduate student.<ref name="jimorjack">{{Cite web|url=https://alumni.harvard.edu/stories/riddiford-and-truman|title=Lynn Riddiford '58 and James Truman PhD '70|date=11 February 2014|website=Harvard Alumni|access-date=2 June 2018}}</ref> Riddiford and Truman retired from Janelia Research Campus in 2016 and moved back to the University of Washington setting up their laboratory at the [[Friday Harbor Laboratories]], Friday Harbor, Washington.
